title: Rook against two connected pawns
summary: When two pawns beat the rook, how rook and king stop them, and counting the tempi.
part.count.title: No kings: count the steps
part.count.summary: On the sixth, two connected pawns beat the rook; on the fifth, the rook to move attacks from the side and wins.
part.behind.title: Behind the leading pawn
part.behind.summary: Before both reach the sixth, the rook goes behind the more advanced one. The check only helps the black king.
part.king.title: The rook's king counts the squares
part.king.summary: With your king close, the rook wins even against pawns on the sixth. One square farther, and it loses.
part.kingFirst.title: King first, capture later
part.kingFirst.summary: The pawn held by the rook is not going anywhere: the king comes first, and the capture arrives with tempo.
part.checks.title: The check that gains a tempo
part.checks.summary: When your king is one tempo short, a check sends the black king away from the pawn that matters, and the rook saves the draw, even by giving itself up.
part.escort.title: The king escorts the pawns
part.escort.summary: From the other side: the king goes first and hides from the checks, and the pawns move together.
part.shoulder.title: The shoulder and the detour
part.shoulder.summary: The pawns' king blocks the rook's king from the front; the rook's king goes around the side.
part.recap.title: Summary
part.recap.summary: The lesson's rules and the practical challenge.
step.t_fifth: Black's pawns are on their fifth rank, on f4 and g4, and both kings are far away, on a8 and h8. One step further, on the sixth, two connected pawns would already beat the lone rook: that is Euwe's rule. Here each still needs three steps, and it is the rook's move. Is there a winning move?
step.t_fifth.hint1: The pawns need three steps. The rook has one tempo to use before they move.
step.t_fifth.hint2: Look for a square from which the rook attacks both pawns at once.
step.fifth: 1.Ra4! On the pawns' rank, the rook attacks both from the side. Side by side, one pawn does not protect the other, because a pawn only protects diagonally forward. Whatever Black plays, one of them falls, and the survivor is left alone against the rook. Any other move draws or loses.
step.d_fifth: Watch the rook pick off a pawn.
step.d_fifth.m1: 1.Ra4: both pawns are attacked. If one advances, the rook captures the other.
step.d_fifth.m2: 1...Kg7: the black king runs to help, but it is still far from the pawns.
step.d_fifth.m3: 2.Rxf4. One pawn down. After 2...g3, 3.Rg4+ puts the rook behind the last pawn, with check, and your king comes to collect it.
step.sixthFifth: The same position, but now it is Black to move. 1...f3! One pawn reaches the sixth before the rook can move. The rook still captures a pawn, but only draws: after 2.Rh1+ Kg7 3.Rg1 Kf6 4.Rxg4 Ke5, the black king reaches the f-pawn in time. On the fifth, whoever has the move decides.
step.recapMove: On the other side of the board: the pawns are on the fifth, the kings far away, and the rook to move. Win.
step.recapMove.hint: On the pawns' rank, the rook attacks both from the side.
step.recapMove.done: 1.Rh4! Then 2.Rxc4. Attacked from the side, the pawns cannot protect each other, and the survivor is left alone for the rook to catch from behind.
step.t_behind: Now the pawns are not side by side: the c-pawn has already reached its sixth rank, on c3, and the b-pawn is still on the fifth, on b4. Your king is far away, on h1, and the black king is on h7. The rook could give check on a7, or do something else. What do you play?
step.t_behind.hint1: The check attacks nothing. Where does it send the black king?
step.t_behind.hint2: Look for a square from which the rook holds the most advanced pawn from behind.
step.behind: 1.Rc6! The rook goes behind the most advanced pawn. From c6 it watches the whole path of the c3-pawn down to c1 and attacks it too. The b4-pawn protects c3, but if it advances it stops protecting it; and the c3-pawn cannot move without falling. Both are frozen while your king comes. It is the only winning move.
step.d_behind: Watch the frozen pawns fall one by one.
step.d_behind.m1: 1.Rc6: behind the c-pawn, which can no longer move without falling.
step.d_behind.m2: 1...b3: the b-pawn runs, and the c-pawn is left unprotected.
step.d_behind.m3: 2.Rxc3: the rook captures and, on the same rank, already attacks b3. The black king is too far away to save the pawn: rook against king, and the rest is technique.
step.behindCheck: And the check 1.Ra7+? It attacks nothing, and the black king does not go back: it heads for the pawns. After 1...Kg6 2.Rc7 Kf5 3.Rc4 Ke5 4.Rxb4 Kd5, the rook has won a pawn, but the black king has reached the other one, and it is a draw. The check pushed the black king closer to the pawns.
step.behindMove: Now the black king is closer, on f7. Win the same way.
step.behindMove.hint: Before thinking of a check, look at the most advanced pawn, and at the square behind it.
step.behindMove.done: 1.Rc6! With the rook behind c3, both pawns are frozen. After 1...Ke7 your king starts walking, 2.Kg2, and the black king doesn't arrive in time to free them.
step.t_king: Black's pawns are on their sixth rank, on f3 and g3, where the lone rook can no longer hold. But now your king is on c4, and the black king is far away, on h8. With your king close, what is the plan?
step.t_king.hint1: Count how many moves your king needs to stand next to the squares the pawns will pass.
step.t_king.hint2: The pawns need two moves to reach the first rank. The rook on a1 already watches that whole rank.
step.king: With the king close, the rook wins. It stays where it is, guarding the first rank, and the king runs diagonally: 1.Kd3, heading for e2 and e3, next to the pawns. Together, king and rook do what the rook alone couldn't: the king guards the promotion squares the rook doesn't cover and attacks the pawns up close. But count square by square: with the king one square further away, on b4, the pawns arrive first, and it loses. Fine and Benko sum it up: with the rook's king far away, two pawns win; with it close, the rook wins.
step.d_king: Watch the king arrive in time. Notice the rook doesn't move: it is already doing its job on a1.
step.d_king.m1: 1.Kd3: diagonally, towards the squares in front of the pawns.
step.d_king.m2: 1...g2: the pawn threatens g1, but the rook covers that square.
step.d_king.m3: 2.Ke3! The king attacks f3 and watches f2. The pawns are frozen: the f-pawn falls next, and the g-pawn too, because the rook watches g1. King and rook against king.
step.kingMove: Now your king is on c3. Count the squares and arrive in time.
step.kingMove.hint: Count the squares to e2: the shortest road is the one that arrives in time. The rook stays where it is until the king arrives.
step.kingMove.done: In time. The king holds f1 and the f-pawn, and the rook does the rest. Here 1.Kd2, 1.Kd3 and 1.Kd4 win, and so does the check 1.Rh1+; but 1.Kc2 or 1.Kb3 lost, because they do not reach e2 in time.
step.t_kingFirst: Now Black's pawns are split. The g-pawn is already on its seventh rank, on g2, one step from promotion, with the rook behind it on g8. The b-pawn is on b4, with the black king next to it on c3. Your king is on f3. Capturing g2 looks obvious. Do you capture?
step.t_kingFirst.hint1: Can g2 promote? What happens to the new queen on g1?
step.t_kingFirst.hint2: Count the b-pawn's steps after the capture, and see where the black king will be.
step.kingFirst: 1.Ke2! The g2-pawn is not going anywhere: if it promotes, the rook captures the new queen on g1. The danger is the b-pawn, with the black king beside it. So your king goes first, towards it, and the capture of g2 waits until it comes with tempo. It is the only winning move.
step.d_kingFirst: Watch the king go first, and the capture come at the right moment.
step.d_kingFirst.m1: 1.Ke2: the king heads for the b-pawn. The g2-pawn is still held by the rook.
step.d_kingFirst.m2: 1...Kc2: the black king goes to escort the b-pawn and takes d1, d2 and d3 away from your king.
step.d_kingFirst.m3: 2.Rxg2: now the capture. Notice the rook is on the second rank, the same as the black king, with your king in between.
step.d_kingFirst.m4: 2...b3: the pawn runs, protected by the king.
step.d_kingFirst.m5: 3.Ke1+! The king steps aside and the rook gives a discovered check. The black king must answer the check, and the rook gains the tempo to catch the b-pawn.
step.kingFirstGreedy: And the greedy capture 1.Rxg2? It spends the tempo the king needed: 1...b3 2.Rg1 b2 3.Rb1 Kc2, the black king attacks the rook, and after 4.Rxb2+ Kxb2 nothing is left. Draw.
step.kingFirstMove: Now your king is farther away, on f4, and the black king is on c4. The g2-pawn is still held. Which way?
step.kingFirstMove.hint: King first, towards e2. The capture can wait.
step.kingFirstMove.done: 1.Ke3, 2.Ke2 and only then 3.Rxg2: the g2-pawn waited, and the capture came with the discovered check 4.Ke1+ saved for the right moment.
step.t_checks: Black's pawns are on their sixth rank, on f3 and g3, with the black king next to them on g4. Your king is close, on g6, but not close enough: it is one tempo short, and here the goal is to save the draw. How does the rook win that tempo?
step.t_checks.hint1: Think about where the black king is worst placed.
step.t_checks.hint2: A check can send the black king away from the pawn that matters.
step.checks: 1.Ra4+! The check gains a tempo, and the black king has only one square: h3. There it stands on the edge, far from the f-pawn. Next the rook goes behind that pawn, and your king reaches the g-pawn. Any other move loses.
step.d_checks: Watch the rook and the king work together.
step.d_checks.m1: 1.Ra4+: the check, which leaves the black king a single square.
step.d_checks.m2: 1...Kh3: the only square. From here the black king helps the g-pawn, but not the f-pawn.
step.d_checks.m3: 2.Rf4: the rook goes behind the f-pawn, which nobody protects.
step.d_checks.m4: 2...f2: the pawn advances so as not to fall.
step.d_checks.m5: 3.Kg5: the king comes for the g-pawn. That was the missing tempo. After 3...f1=Q 4.Rxf1 g2 5.Ra1, the rook watches the first rank and your king is close to the last pawn: a draw.
step.checksMove: Now the pawns are on c3 and d3, and the black king on c4. Find the check that gains the tempo, and then the right place for the rook.
step.checksMove.hint: A check along the fourth rank leaves the black king a single square.
step.checksMove.done: 1.Rh4+! Kb3 2.Rd4: the black king went away from the d-pawn, and the rook got behind it. Your king arrives, and it is a draw.
step.sacrifice: Sometimes the check is not enough, and the rook has to give itself up. Black's pawns are on d2 and e2. Capturing d2 with the king loses: after 1.Kxd2 exf1=Q, the e-pawn captures the rook and promotes. Any other move loses too: one of the pawns promotes. 1.Rf4+!! The rook leaves f1 with check, on a square where the black king can capture it. After 1...Kxf4, 2.Kxd2 watches e1, and the e-pawn falls.
step.sacrificeMove: Now it is your turn. The rook on f1 is in the e-pawn's sights, and d2 is one step from promoting. Save the draw.
step.sacrificeMove.hint: The rook has to leave f1 without giving Black time. The black king may even capture it: what matters is where it ends up.
step.sacrificeMove.done: 1.Rf4+!! The rook gave itself up with check. After 1...Kxf4 2.Kxd2, the black king is far from e1, your king watches the promotion square, and the e-pawn falls. A draw.
step.t_escort: Switch sides: now you have the pawns, with your king close, and the black king is far away. The black rook will give checks. What is the way to promote?
step.t_escort.hint1: If you push 1.g6 right away, see which check the rook gives and what it captures.
step.t_escort.hint2: Look for a square for the king where the rook can't reach it with checks, and only then push.
step.escort: 1.Kg6! The king goes before the pawns, heading for h7. On h7, in front of the h-pawn, it is sheltered: the rook can't check along the h-file, because the pawn itself blocks it, and the g-pawn is free to move. Haste spoils everything: 1.g6? After 1...Rh5+, the rook gains the tempo it needed. Draw.
step.d_escort: Watch the king go to its shelter before the pawns move.
step.d_escort.m1: 1.Kg6! The king protects both pawns and heads for h7.
step.d_escort.m2: 1...Kc7: the black king runs, but it is too far away.
step.d_escort.m3: 2.Kh7: the shelter. The rook has no check, because the h-pawn blocks the file.
step.d_escort.m4: 2...Kd7: the black king keeps coming along the seventh, but it is late.
step.d_escort.m5: 3.g6: now the g-pawn advances. After 3...Ke7 4.g7, the rook will have to give itself up for it.
step.escortMove: Your turn to play like Shankland, against Maghsoodloo, Prague 2022. White's pawns are on a6 and b5, your king on b6 and the black king far away, on e3. The black rook is waiting for a chance to get behind a pawn. King or pawn?
step.escortMove.hint: The king in front of the a-pawn. It is the b-pawn that will move.
step.escortMove.done: 75.Ka7! Shankland did not push the a-pawn: after 75.a7? 75...Ra2! The rook gets behind it, and it is a draw. Maghsoodloo, almost out of time, replied 75...Rc8, and after 76.b6 there was no defence left: the king guards b8, and the b-pawn walks all the way.
step.connect: Your pawns are far apart: the e-pawn is already on e6, the f-pawn stayed on f4. The black king is far away, on h2. Before running with the front one, bring them together.
step.connect.hint: The rear pawn moves up to protect the front one.
step.connect.done: 1.f5! Now f5 protects e6, and the two move together with the king alongside: after 1...Rf1 2.Ke5 Kg3 3.f6, f6 protects the coming e7, and the rook cannot stop both. The hasty 1.e7? After 1...Re1+, the rook is behind the pawn, and it is a draw.
step.kingBefore: Now you play the black pawns, and the white rook is behind them, on c5, attacking c3. The white king is far away, on g6. Pawn or king?
step.kingBefore.hint: With the rook behind, the king moves first: in front of the pawn it attacks.
step.kingBefore.done: 1...Kc2! The king stands in front of the c-pawn and protects it, and the d-pawn walks with an escort: after 2.Ra5, 2...d3. The mistake is 1...c2? The rook waits behind and captures the new queen: 2.Rc6 c1=Q 3.Rxc1, only one pawn is left, and it is a draw.
step.t_shoulder: You have Black's pawns, on f4 and g5, and your king on f5. The white rook is far away, on a8, and the white king comes through the centre, from c5. On their own, the pawns do not arrive before it, and the goal is the draw. Pawn or king?
step.t_shoulder.hint1: Which way does the white king want to go to reach the pawns?
step.t_shoulder.hint2: A king cannot stand next to the other king.
step.shoulder: 1...Ke4! Your king steps into the white king's path. On e4 it takes away d4 and d3, the squares the white king would come back through. It is the shoulder: one king blocks the other without touching the pawns. Pushing at once loses. After 1...g4? 2.Kd4! the white king gets back in time.
step.d_shoulder: Watch the shoulder hold the white king back.
step.d_shoulder.m1: 1...Ke4: the shoulder. The white king cannot pass through d4 or d3.
step.d_shoulder.m2: 2.Ra1: the rook comes to the first rank, waiting for the pawns.
step.d_shoulder.m3: 2...f3: now the pawn moves, with the king beside it.
step.d_shoulder.m4: 3.Re1+: a check to move the black king out of the way.
step.d_shoulder.m5: 3...Kd3! The king stays in front of the white king. After 4.Rd1+ Ke2 it protects f1, the f-pawn walks, and it is a draw.
step.shoulderGame: Nabaty against Zelcic, Malinska 2014, at the end of a wild game. The white king, on d7, is far from the pawns, and Black drew without any calculation with 82...Kf5!, the shoulder: the black king stands in front of the white one and takes away e6 and e5. Zelcic played 82...Ke5 and, after 83.Ke7, tried to promote both pawns with 83...f5? The pawn took his own king's best square, and White went on to win.
step.around: Now from the rook's side: the black king, on d6, blocks the centre. Your king is on b7. Which way does it reach the pawns?
step.around.hint: Around the side, where the black king can't reach. A check would only push it forward.
step.around.done: 1.Kb6! The king walks down the b-file: after 1...d4 2.Kb5 Kd5 3.Kb4, it reaches the pawns from the side. The shoulder blocks the front; the side was open. The check 1.Ra6+? only drew.
step.recap: To take to your games. Without kings, count the steps: on the sixth, two connected pawns beat the rook; on the fifth, the rook to move attacks both from the side. Before both reach the sixth, the rook goes behind the most advanced pawn; check only if it gains a tempo.
step.rules: On the rook's side, the king counts the squares, comes before the capture and goes around the shoulder. On the pawns' side, the king goes first and hides from the checks, blocks the rook's king with its shoulder, and the rear pawn moves up before the front one runs.
step.push: One last time from the pawns' side, already on the sixth, with no kings nearby. The rook on a3 attacks only the f3-pawn, which has no protection. Don't waste time on it or on the king: push.
step.push.hint: The attacked pawn can step out of the attack and be protected by the other one. Then the other one runs too.
step.push.done: A new queen. After 1...f2 2.Rf3 g2, the rook was too late: with the pawns on the sixth, each of their moves is a threat, and the rook can only answer one.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge. Black's pawns are on the sixth, on b3 and c3, the black king on f5, far from them, and your king on e1. Count the squares, bring the king and win.
ex.e06: Black to play and win. From the game Parligras against Gopal, Gibraltar 2012. The pawns are well advanced, and the white rook is behind them. Pawn or king?
ex.e06.hint: With the rook behind the pawns, the king is the one that must help first.
ex.e06.solution: 60...Ka2! The king steps in front of the a-pawn and guards b3 and b2. Now the b-pawn walks with an escort, and the white king arrives too late. That is what Gopal played. If 60...a2 instead, White brings the king in time and it is a draw: a2 is the pawn that no longer needed to move.
ex.e12: White to play and win. Now you have the pawns against the black rook, with your king close and the black one far away. What is the move?
ex.e12.hint: One pawn is alone in front, the other stayed behind. How do they start protecting each other?
ex.e12.solution: 1.h5! The back pawn comes closer and now protects the one on g6. The two walk together, with the king alongside, and the rook can't stop both. The hasty 1.g7 allows 1...Rg1, the rook behind the pawn, and the h-pawn is too far back: a draw. King moves give the rook the time it needed. Position from Mavens's study on Lichess.
ex.e13: White to play and win. The pawns are not both on the sixth yet, but one of them is already there. A check or another move?
ex.e13.hint: The check attacks nothing. Look for a square where the rook attacks a pawn from behind.
ex.e13.solution: 1.Rg6! The rook goes behind the g-pawn. After 1...Kd7, 2.Rg4! attacks both, and after 2...g2, 3.Rxg2: the f-pawn is alone and the black king is far away. The check 1.Ra7+ looks natural but only draws; king moves like 1.Ka7 allow 1...f3, both pawns on the sixth, and lose. From Audax6's study on Lichess.
ex.e14: White to play and win. From the game Leko against Markowski, Polanica Zdroj 1998. Now the pawns are split. The h-pawn is right there to be taken. Do you take it?
ex.e14.hint: The h-pawn isn't going anywhere: the rook watches it along the h-file. Which pawn is really running, and who can catch it?
ex.e14.solution: 66.Kf2!! The king first. The h-pawn is held by the rook and the king, and the danger is the c-pawn. After 66...Kd2, 67.Rxh2 (or 67.Kf1): now the rook takes with your king one step away, and the discovered 68.Kf1+ wins the missing tempo. The greedy 66.Rxh2? loses that tempo: 66...c3, 67...c2 and 68...Kd2, and the c-pawn with its king alongside is worth a draw. Leko played 66.Kf2.
ex.e16: White to play and win. From the game Nabaty against Zelcic, Malinska 2014. The pawns are on the fifth and the black king stands right in front of yours. Which way does your king come back?
ex.e16.hint: Through the front, the black king bars the way. The pawns don't protect the squares behind them.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Kf7! The king goes around the pawns from behind, along the g-file. After 1...g4, 2.Kg6 (or 2.Rc1), and the king reaches the pawns where the black king can't get in the way. Checks don't help: the game went 1.Rc5+, and with 1...Kf4! the black king would have barred the white one and drawn. 1.Kf7 is the only winning move.
ex.e15: Black to play and draw. From the game Shankland against Gao, Doha 2014. Your two pawns can't reach the first rank before the white king comes back. How do you hold?
ex.e15.hint: You don't need both pawns: one costing the rook is enough. Before pushing, look at the white king's path.
ex.e15.solution: 40...Ke5! Your king stands in the white king's path, shouldering it away. After 41.Kc5, 41...h4; after 42.Kc4, 42...Ke4, always in the way. When the rook gets behind one pawn (43.Rh7), push the other: 43...g5. The rook takes one pawn, the other costs the rook, and it is a draw. Every move was the only one. Pushing 40...h4 right away loses: 41.Kd5! and the white king gets back in time. That is how Gao held against Shankland.
ex.e17: White to play and draw. A study by Ladislav Prokeš, 1939. The black pawns are on the sixth, with their king next to them, and your king is far away. There are four only moves to the draw.
ex.e17.hint: The rook alone can't hold. The king has to reach the pawns, and the rook can buy it time, even by giving itself up.
ex.e17.solution: 1.Kg4! The king comes first; checks right away lose. After 1...e2, 2.Rc1+! (to 2...Kd4) and 3.Kf3! The king attacks e2. After 3...d2, 4.Rc4+!! The rook gives itself up: 4...Kxc4 and 5.Kxe2. The white king stands in front of the d-pawn and the draw is safe. Notice that no white move had an alternative: this is Prokeš's manoeuvre.
ex.e18: White to play and win. A study by Richard Réti. Now there are three pawns on the second rank, but your king is right among them. Which pawn first?
ex.e18.hint: Taking a pawn at once looks obvious, but watch the tempo. One king square holds two pawns at the same time.
ex.e18.solution: 1.Kf2! The king watches e1 and g1 at once. After 1...Ke4, 2.Kxe2: two split pawns are left. Now the rook attacks the g-pawn along the g-file (3.Rg1; 3.Ra1, 3.Re1 and 3.Kd2 also win), and after 3...Ke4, 4.Re1 (or 4.Ra1, 4.Rc1): the black king can't stay close to both pawns. 1.Kxg2? allows 1...Ke4, the e-pawn goes with tempo and the black king reaches the c-pawn: a draw; 1.Rxc2? loses.
key.sixth: Two connected pawns on the sixth rank with both kings far away: the rook alone cannot hold. Any White move loses.
key.fifth: One rank earlier, the rook still wins, but only if it is its move and it attacks the pawns from the side. With Black to move, it is a draw.
key.king: The rook's king counts too: here it is close enough and the rook wins. One square further away, and the pawns get through.
key.euwe: Euwe's rule: two connected pawns on the sixth rank are worth a rook. Black is to move and cannot stop them.
key.escort: The king walks with the pawns and hides from the checks in front of them; only then does the right pawn advance.
key.resource: The pawns are almost there, but the rook still draws: instead of chasing them, it threatens to mate the black king.
history: Two connected pawns, side by side, can be stronger than a rook: once they get close to promoting, each protects the other and the rook alone cannot cope. This ending has no famous discoverer, but it has practical rules that are passed from book to book. World champion Max Euwe and Walter Meiden wrote that two connected pawns on the sixth rank are worth a rook; Reuben Fine and Pal Benko added that it all depends on where the rook's king is. The count is tight, and often a single move changes the result. The ending turns up in grandmaster games too, such as Shankland against Maghsoodloo in Prague, 2022, where the king escorted the pawns all the way.
practice: Now the practical challenge: rook against two pawns on the sixth, with your king close to them and the black king far away. Count the squares and win.
